blocks.content: The previous topic covered first normal form, requiring every column to hold a single atomic value, second normal form, 2NF, builds directly on top of that, addressing a different problem, columns that depend on only part of a composite key rather than the whole thing.

This topic covers what a partial dependency actually means, a concrete violation using the enrollments example from the earlier Candidate and Composite Keys topic, and why 2NF only becomes relevant once a table has a composite primary key.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438610006-166051545.png
1. What Second Normal Form Requires

A table satisfies 2NF when it is already in 1NF, and every non key column depends on the entire primary key, not just part of it, this rule only becomes relevant for tables with a composite primary key, covered in the earlier Candidate and Composite Keys topic, a single column primary key cannot have a partial dependency by definition.
2. Full Dependency on a Composite Key
blocks.text: 2. Full Dependency on a Composite Key

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438610006-933902259.png
blocks.alt: Full Dependency on a Composite Key

blocks.content: Suppose an enrollments table has a composite primary key of student_id and course_id, a column genuinely satisfies 2NF only if you need both parts of that key to determine its value, a grade column depends on both, which specific student, in which specific course, so it is fully dependent, no violation there.
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438610203-725462137.png
blocks.alt: Full Dependency on a Composite Key

blocks.content: 3. A Concrete Partial Dependency Violation
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438610204-11610666.png

Now suppose that same enrollments table also includes a student_name column, student_name only depends on student_id, it has nothing to do with which course, that is a partial dependency, student_name only needs part of the composite key to be determined, and this violates 2NF.

-- Violates 2NF: student_name depends only on part of the composite key
student_id | course_id | student_name | grade
1          | 101       | Aisha Khan   | A
1          | 102       | Aisha Khan   | B

blocks.content: 4. Why This Causes the Same Anomalies as Before
blocks.text: 4. Why This Causes the Same Anomalies as Before

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438610205-830155186.png
blocks.alt: Why This Causes the Same Anomalies as Before

blocks.content: This is exactly the same redundancy problem covered in the earlier Why Normalization topic, student_name is repeated once for every course that student takes, updating it correctly means updating every single enrollment row for that student, missing one creates an inconsistent, contradictory record.

{"headers":["Column","Depends On","2NF Status"],"rows":[["grade","student_id and course_id together","Fully dependent, satisfies 2NF"],["student_name","student_id alone","Partially dependent, violates 2NF"]]}
5. The Fix, Moving the Column to Its Own Table
blocks.text: 5. The Fix, Moving the Column to Its Own Table

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438610206-784137621.png
blocks.alt: The Fix, Moving the Column to Its Own Table

blocks.content: The fix is moving student_name out of the enrollments table entirely, into a students table where it genuinely belongs, keyed by student_id alone, the enrollments table keeps only the columns that truly depend on the full composite key, grade in this case.
The corrected structure
6. Why Single Column Keys Cannot Violate 2NF
blocks.text: 6. Why Single Column Keys Cannot Violate 2NF

blocks.content: /engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438610207-163894798.png
blocks.alt: Why Single Column Keys Cannot Violate 2NF

blocks.content: A table with a single column primary key, an ordinary surrogate id for instance, automatically satisfies 2NF, since there is no way for a column to depend on only part of a key that has just one part, 2NF is specifically a concern for tables with composite keys, exactly the kind covered in the earlier Candidate and Composite Keys topic.

blocks.title: This is why 2NF is easy to overlook
blocks.content: Most tables in a typical schema use a single column surrogate key and never encounter a 2NF violation at all, it specifically shows up in junction tables representing many to many relationships that also carry extra descriptive columns.
7. Recognizing a 2NF Violation in Practice

A practical way to spot a 2NF violation is asking, for each non key column, could I determine this value knowing only part of the composite key, if the answer is yes, that column has a partial dependency and belongs in a different table.

{"headers":["1NF","2NF"],"rows":[["Every column holds a single atomic value","Builds on 1NF, adds full dependency on the whole key"],["Applies to every table","Only relevant when a table has a composite primary key"]]}
/engineering/library/dbms/images/1785438610207-252569155.png

blocks.title: 2NF sits between 1NF and 3NF for a reason
blocks.content: Each normal form in this sequence assumes the previous one already holds, 2NF specifically assumes the table is already in 1NF before its own rule about full key dependency even applies.
8. Common Mistakes

["Adding a descriptive column, like a name or a fixed price, to a junction table where it only depends on part of the composite key","Assuming 2NF applies to every table, when it is only relevant to tables with a composite primary key","Fixing the partial dependency but forgetting the foreign key relationship back to the new table","Confusing a full dependency, like grade depending on both student_id and course_id, with a partial one"]
items: Adding a descriptive column, like a name or a fixed price, to a junction table where it only depends on part of the composite key
Assuming 2NF applies to every table, when it is only relevant to tables with a composite primary key
Fixing the partial dependency but forgetting the foreign key relationship back to the new table
Confusing a full dependency, like grade depending on both student_id and course_id, with a partial one

blocks.content: 9. Key Takeaways

["Second normal form requires 1NF plus full dependency of every column on the entire composite key, not just part of it","2NF only matters for tables with a composite primary key, single column keyed tables satisfy it automatically","The fix for a partial dependency is always the same, move the affected column into its own table keyed by the part of the key it actually depends on","The next topic, Third Normal Form, addresses a different kind of dependency problem, one that can happen even in single column keyed tables"]
items: Second normal form requires 1NF plus full dependency of every column on the entire composite key, not just part of it
2NF only matters for tables with a composite primary key, single column keyed tables satisfy it automatically
The fix for a partial dependency is always the same, move the affected column into its own table keyed by the part of the key it actually depends on
The next topic, Third Normal Form, addresses a different kind of dependency problem, one that can happen even in single column keyed tables
